subject: geography

moments.title: Essay on the Principle of Population
moments.who: Thomas Robert Malthus, English clergyman and economist
moments.body: Malthus publishes his Essay anonymously. The argument: population tends to grow geometrically while food supply grows arithmetically, so population is held in check by 'positive' (famine, disease, war) and 'preventive' (delayed marriage) checks. Revised across five further editions to 1826.

quote.text: Population, when unchecked, increases in a geometrical ratio. Subsistence increases only in an arithmetical ratio.
quote.attrib: Malthus, Essay on the Principle of Population, 1798

moments.takeaway: Malthus was writing against Enlightenment optimism (Godwin, Condorcet) about indefinite human improvement.

moments.title: Demographic Transition Model
moments.body: Thompson (1929) and Notestein (1945) develop the Demographic Transition Model: pre-industrial societies have high birth and death rates; industrialising societies show declining death rates first, then birth rates; mature industrial societies have low rates of both.
moments.takeaway: The DTM remains a staple of A-level geography. Stage 4 (low birth, low death) is now extended to Stage 5 (declining population) in many developed countries.

moments.title: Population Bomb
moments.body: Ehrlich's 'The Population Bomb' (1968) revives Malthusian fears: 'The battle to feed all of humanity is over. In the 1970s hundreds of millions of people will starve to death.' Famines did not occur on this scale — Green Revolution agriculture (Norman Borlaug, IR8 rice 1966) transformed yields.
moments.takeaway: Neo-Malthusian arguments recur (Limits to Growth 1972, peak oil debates) and are repeatedly modified by technological change.

now.title: From boom to bust
now.body: World population is around 8 billion (2022 milestone) and expected to peak around 10 billion mid-century before declining. Most developed countries have below-replacement fertility. The 21st-century demographic story is increasingly about ageing and decline, not Malthusian overshoot.
now.open_questions: Is the Earth's carrying capacity finite? Most current estimates think so but the binding constraint is more often water, soil, biodiversity or atmospheric CO2 than food production capacity.

reflection: Malthus has been wrong about timing but right about asking the question. Carrying capacity, food security, and the relationship between population and resources are still live geographical questions — just with shifting binding constraints.
